title: Raga or popular tune
hookLine: some sing kirtan strictly in ragas, others in simpler tunes; both are loved

lines: A SLOW RAGA. A SIMPLE TUNE.
cards: Two gurdwaras, a few streets apart, on the same evening. In the first, a raagi with a harmonium and a tabla player opens a hymn slowly, notes rising in a set order, a mood held a long while before the words begin.
In the second, teenagers sing the same hymn to a simple tune you could hum after one hearing, and the whole hall sings back. Both are kirtan. Both are the Gurus' words.
So which way is right? Sikhs have argued about it with real care, and that's today's question: raga or popular tune.

teach.h: THE BOOK IS BUILT ON RAGAS.
teach.b: First, the book itself is built on ragas. Open the Guru Granth Sahib and the hymns are gathered under raga headings: Sri Raag, Majh, Gauri, Asa, and on through the book.
A raga is more than a scale: a set of notes, a way of moving between them, and a mood the music carries. So some Sikhs say plainly: if a Guru set a hymn in a raga, sing it in that raga.
The music is part of the message, and changing it loses something the Guru chose. Second, the other side. Others say what matters is that the words reach people.
A simple tune lets a whole hall sing, a child learn a hymn by heart on the way home, a newcomer join on the very first night.

teach.h: A TUNE THAT OPENS THE DOOR.
teach.b: For them, a tune that opens the door is doing the Guru's work. Third, what the scripture says about ragas themselves.
In a var in Sri Raag, Guru Amar Das names Sri Raag as the finest of the ragas, and adds the condition in the same breath.
In paraphrase: it is finest if, through it, a person holds love for the truth. Even the praise of a raga is tied to love.
Fourth, both are loved. Some gurdwaras keep strict raga kirtan; others sing simpler tunes; some sangats hear both in one week. Those who keep the ragas guard something precious.
Those who sing simply open a door.
The line from Sri Raag sits over both: the music serves the love, not the other way around.

how: Some gurdwaras and kirtan schools sing hymns in the ragas named in the Guru Granth Sahib; others use simpler tunes so the whole sangat can join, and some sangats hear both.

games.why: the praise comes with a condition in the same breath: finest if, through it, a person holds love for the truth. the music serves the love.

practice: If you can, play a short stretch of raga kirtan and then a hymn sung to a simple tune; if not, recall one slow piece you know and one you could hum after a single hearing. Don't rank them.
Notice what each asks of you: the slow one asks you to wait, the simple one invites you to join.

wordCard.voice: Raga or popular tune. The question of how to sing the Gurus' hymns: in the ragas the book names, or in simple tunes a whole hall can sing. Sikhs hold both. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: a raga, the musical mode each section of the Guru Granth Sahib is set in.
